title: Is Now a Good Time to Buy a Home in Middle Tennessee?
description: Is now a good time to buy a home? A plain look at Middle Tennessee data, mortgage rates and your own budget, with no predictions or hype.
keyword: is now a good time to buy
body:
People ask me this question more than any other, and I understand why. A home is a big purchase, and the headlines pull in every direction.

I can't tell you where prices or rates will go, and nobody else can reliably do it either. What I can do is show you what the local numbers say today, how to think about timing, and what usually matters more than the calendar.

## What the local numbers show right now

{{img:0}}

Start with the numbers closest to home. For the Nashville metro area, the four weeks ending 2026-09-27 showed a median sale price of $462,304, according to the [Redfin Data Center](https://www.redfin.com/news/data-center/). Homes took a median of 68 days to sell, sold for 97.8% of list price on average, and 2,489 homes sold in that stretch.

The same Redfin data showed 5.4 months of supply. Months of supply is how long it would take to sell every active listing at the current pace of sales. Under 4 months favors sellers, 4 to 6 months is balanced, and over 6 months favors buyers. At 5.4, the metro sits in the balanced range.

For the city of Nashville, Redfin's rolling three-month data as of 2026-08-31 showed a median sale price of $477,500, down 0.1% from a year earlier. Median days on market was 64, the average sale-to-list ratio was 97.6%, and there were 4,850 active listings with 5.3 months of supply. The metro and city figures cover different areas and time windows, so don't expect them to match.

Other sources point the same general way. Zillow Research had its Market Temperature Index at 44 for Nashville, down 6 over three months, and rated the market as leaning toward buyers. Realtor.com Research put Davidson County's hotness score at 16.6 out of 100. Taken together, these describe a market that has cooled. That is a description of recent data, not a forecast.

If you want the same kind of figures for the I-65 corridor, the [market data page](/market-data) is a good place to look.

## The mortgage rate question

Rates are the other half of the picture. Freddie Mac's 30-year fixed rate was 7.28% for the week of 2026-10-01, as reported through FRED at the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. That affects your monthly payment more than a small change in price does.

Many buyers wait for rates to fall before buying. The trouble is that waiting is a bet in either direction. If rates drop, you may be glad you waited. If they rise, or prices move up, or the home you wanted sells to someone else, waiting costs you. Rent paid in the meantime is a real cost too, even though it is easy to overlook.

Some buyers plan to buy now and refinance later if rates fall. That is a possibility, not a plan. A refinance depends on rates, credit, home value and income at that time, and it has its own closing costs.

You can test different rates and prices with the [mortgage calculator](/mortgage-calculator) to see what a payment looks like before you commit to anything.

## Two ways to think about timing

{{img:1}}

The older approach is to try to time the market or the seasons. Listings and buyer activity do vary by time of year. But for any one household, the right moment usually depends more on its own finances, timeline and the specific home than on the calendar.

A newer approach is to focus on readiness and monthly budget:

- Stable income
- An emergency fund that is still intact after closing
- A total payment that fits comfortably, including taxes, insurance and maintenance

The second approach also favors local data over national headlines. Months of supply, days on market and sale-to-list ratio for your own city tell you more than a national story does, because conditions can differ a lot between cities and price ranges.

Another useful framing is to compare the full monthly cost of buying with the monthly cost of renting a comparable home, and to weigh how long you expect to stay. If you are likely to move within a short time, that changes the math.

## Options buyers ask about

When rates feel high, buyers often ask what can soften the payment. A few things come up. None are guaranteed, and a lender has to confirm what is allowed for your loan.

- **Seller concessions.** You can ask the seller to pay some closing costs or to fund a temporary or permanent rate buydown. Whether that is possible depends on the seller, the home and the market.
- **Adjustable-rate mortgages.** An ARM has a rate that is fixed for an initial period and can then change. It can lower the early payment but carries the risk of higher payments later. The [CFPB Owning a Home guides](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/owning-a-home/) explain how ARMs work in plain language.
- **Assumable loans.** Some existing FHA and VA loans are assumable, meaning a qualified buyer may take over the seller's terms with lender approval. They are uncommon, so ask, but don't count on finding one.
- **State programs.** The [Tennessee Housing Development Agency](https://www.thda.org) offers home loan programs through participating lenders, so ask any lender you consider whether they take part.

It also helps to get Loan Estimates from more than one lender. The CFPB encourages this because rates and fees can differ. The Loan Estimate is a standard three-page form, so you can compare them side by side. You choose your own lender, and you are free to use any lender you like.

## So, is now a good time to buy?

The honest answer is that it depends on you. The local data shows a market in the balanced range that has cooled recently, with a mortgage rate of 7.28%. Whether that works depends on your savings, your monthly budget, how long you plan to stay and whether the right home is available.

If you are weighing it, a good first step is a conversation about your numbers, not a prediction about the market. Remember too that school assignment and property taxes depend on the exact address, so check those with the school district and the county for any home you get serious about.

If you'd like to talk it through, fill out the [Get Matched form](/buy#form) and I will schedule a call. You will be talking with me within the next 48 hours. You can also reach me through the [contact page](/contact) with any question, no matter how early you are in the process.

faq.q: Is now a good time to buy a home in Nashville?
faq.a: It depends on your finances, timeline and the specific home. Redfin showed 5.4 months of supply for the Nashville metro in the four weeks ending 2026-09-27, which falls in the balanced range of 4 to 6 months.

faq.q: What is the current 30-year mortgage rate?
faq.a: Freddie Mac's 30-year fixed rate was 7.28% for the week of 2026-10-01, reported through FRED. Rates change weekly, and your own rate depends on your lender and finances.

faq.q: Should I wait for mortgage rates to fall before buying?
faq.a: Nobody can reliably predict where rates will go, so waiting is a bet in either direction. The cost of waiting, such as rent paid, price changes or losing a home you wanted, is real.

faq.q: What does months of supply mean?
faq.a: It is how long it would take to sell every active listing at the current pace of sales. Under 4 months favors sellers, 4 to 6 months is balanced, and over 6 months favors buyers.

faq.q: Can I refinance later if rates drop?
faq.a: Maybe, but it is not guaranteed. A refinance depends on rates, credit, home value and income at that time, and it has its own closing costs.
